title: The line you haven't drawn
subtitle: Following the resentment back to the boundary it's been pointing at.

steps.body:
There's someone whose behaviour leaves a residue in you — a tightness, the conversation replayed in the shower.

We're not here to decide whether they're wrong. We're here to listen to what the residue is pointing at.

steps.title: Bring one person to mind you quietly resent right now.
steps.body: No need to explain or justify. When you picture the last moment with them — what's the feeling in your body?

steps.title: If the feeling had one word, what is it?
steps.body: Just the felt word underneath it.

steps.title: What do they do that lands as too much, or not fair?
steps.body: Keep it to the concrete moment — the specific thing, not their whole character.

steps.title: How often have you told them, plainly, that it doesn't work for you?
steps.body: Out loud, in words — not hinted. No judgment either way.

Sometimes the people we resent are doing the very thing we haven't let ourselves do — taking up space, saying no, asking plainly.

Not a verdict, just a question worth sitting with: what might they be modelling that you've kept on a short leash in yourself?

steps.title: Finish this: 'The line I haven't drawn is…'
steps.body: The limit the resentment has been pointing at all along.
steps.placeholder: The line I haven't drawn is…

steps.title: Turn it into one small, kind boundary you could actually keep.
steps.body: In your own words: 'If [it happens again], I will [one plain sentence I can say or do].' One occasion, one sentence — small enough to keep.

exit.body:
You found the line the resentment was pointing at, and made it small enough to keep.[[ Your boundary: {reclaim}.]]

If drawing it still feels like too much, that's not failure — the wanting-to and the not-yet are both worth noticing. A kept boundary is a kindness to both of you.
